## 1. Original Population Distribution

<!-- Question 1: What does the original population distribution look like? -->

- **Name / Class:** `r TARGET_DIST`
- **Type:** `r summary_table$pop_shape[1]`
- **Description:** The standard normal distribution is a special and
  simplified type of normal distribution where the mean is 0 and the
  standard deviation is 1. This distribution adheres to the empirical
  rule which states that \~68% of data falls within one standard
  deviation of the mean, \~95% of data falls within two standard
  deviations of the mean and \~99.7% of data falls within three standard
  deviations of the mean. It is also the pillar of the central limit
  theorem and the distribution which we are trying to show other sample
  distributions become as the n of samples gets larger.
  <!-- Describe features: continuity, boundedness, symmetry/skewness, support, unimodal vs multimodal, etc. -->

```{r}
#| label: fig-population-shape
#| fig-cap: "Theoretical / baseline shape of the population distribution (n = 1)."

# Example population plot (n = 1)
# You can customize this plot based on your chosen distribution
ggplot() +
  xlim(-4, 4) +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean=0, sd=1), color = "#009E73", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = paste("Population Density:", TARGET_DIST),
    x = "x",
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 2. Theoretical Mean and Standard Deviation

- **Theoretical Mean (**$\mu$): `r summary_table$theo_mean[1]`
- **Theoretical Standard Deviation (**$\sigma$): 1

For a Standard Normal distribution $X \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$, the PDF
is:

$$f(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\frac{x^2}{2}}$$

The theoretical mean is calculated as:

$$\mu = \text{E}[X] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\frac{x^2}{2}} \, dx = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \left[ -e^{-\frac{x^2}{2}} \right]_{-\infty}^{\infty} = 0$$

The theoretical standard deviation is:

$$\sigma = \sqrt{\text{Var}(X)} = \sqrt{\text{E}[X^2] - (\text{E}[X])^2} = \sqrt{1 - 0^2} = 1$$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 3. Rate of Convergence to Normality

<!-- Question 3: How quickly does the sampling distribution become approximately normal? -->

- **Observations across sample sizes (**$n$): In the graph the red line
  represents kurtosis while the blue line represents skewness. Kurtosis
  is a statistic used to calculate the height of a distribution, where 0
  is standard, and skewness is used to calculate the left or right bias
  that a distribution may have. As we can see here below, both kurtosis
  and skewness are very close to zero throughout the entire set of
  sample sizes.
  <!-- At what sample size n does skewness drop close to 0? Kurtosis near 0? -->

```{r}
#| label: fig-shape-statistics
#| fig-cap: "Convergence of Skewness and Excess Kurtosis toward zero as sample size increases."

shape_data %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(skewness, excess_kurtosis), names_to = "metric", values_to = "value") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = value, color = metric)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(
    title = paste("Shape Statistics vs. n for", TARGET_DIST),
    x = "Sample Size (n)",
    y = "Metric Value",
    color = "Metric"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

::: callout-note
### Important to note

While the kurtosis and skewness plots show a lot of variation, the range
is quite small!
:::

## 4. Simulated Mean vs. Theoretical Mean

The simulated mean and theoretical mean show us if our Monte Carlo
simulation model is behaving as expected.
<!-- Question 4: How does the simulated mean compare with the theoretical mean? -->

```{r}
#| label: tbl-mean-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "Comparison of simulated sample means vs. theoretical mean."

summary_table %>%
  select(n, theo_mean, sim_mean, mean_bias) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("n", "Theoretical Mean (μ)", "Simulated Mean (X̄)", "Mean Bias (X̄ - μ)")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"))
```

- **Analysis:**
  <!-- Does the empirical mean stay close to the theoretical mean across all n? Is there any noticeable bias? -->
  With a general bias of 0 we can say that our model is indeed
  predicting correctly, there is not a large amount of bias in this
  simulation.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 5. Simulated Standard Error vs. Theoretical Standard Error

<!-- Question 5: How does the simulated standard error compare with SE(X̄) = σ / √n? -->

$$\text{SE}(\bar{X}) = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$$

```{r}
#| label: tbl-se-comparison
#| tbl-cap: "Comparison of simulated standard errors with theoretical SE = σ / √n."

summary_table %>%
  select(n, theo_se, sim_se, se_ratio) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("n", "Theoretical SE", "Simulated SE", "SE Ratio (Sim / Theo)")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"))
```

- **Analysis:** With a SE Ratio hovering around 1.0, the empirical
  variability of the simulation matches the theoretical variability.
  This means that the simulation is an ideal benchmark and that we can
  draw conclusions from it.
  <!-- Does the ratio sim_se / theo_se remain close to 1.0? Does the empirical spread decay at rate 1 / √n? -->

## 6. Evidence for Normality

<!-- Question 6: What evidence supports your conclusion that the distribution is—or is not—approximately normal? -->

### Graphical Evidence (Density & Q-Q Plots)

```{r}
#| label: fig-normal-dist-qq
#| fig-cap: "Standardized empirical density and Normal Q-Q plots across selected sample sizes $n$ ($B = 10{,}000$)."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-align: "center"
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(patchwork)

set.seed(8676)

B <- 10000L
# Selected subset of sample sizes to keep layout clean and tight
selected_n <- c(1, 10, 30, 100)

density_qq_list <- list()

for (n_val in selected_n) {
  observations <- rnorm(B * n_val, mean = 0, sd = 1)
  sample_matrix <- matrix(observations, nrow = B, ncol = n_val)
  means <- rowMeans(sample_matrix)
  
  sim_mean <- mean(means)
  sim_se <- sd(means)
  
  z_means <- (means - sim_mean) / sim_se
  density_qq_list[[length(density_qq_list) + 1]] <- data.frame(
    n_label = paste0("n = ", n_val),
    n_num = n_val,
    z = z_means
  )
}

plot_data <- bind_rows(density_qq_list)
plot_data$n_label <- factor(plot_data$n_label, levels = paste0("n = ", selected_n))

# Minimal shared styling for compact plots
tight_theme <- theme_bw(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold", hjust = 0.5),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold"),
    plot.margin = margin(t = 4, r = 6, b = 4, l = 6)
  )

# 1. Density Facets
p_dens_tight <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = z)) +
  geom_density(fill = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.35, color = "#0072B2", linewidth = 0.6) +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = 0, sd = 1), linetype = "dashed", color = "black") +
  facet_wrap(~ n_label, nrow = 2, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Empirical Density vs N(0,1)", x = "Standardized Mean (Z)", y = "Density") +
  tight_theme

# 2. Q-Q Facets
p_qq_tight <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(sample = z)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray30") +
  stat_qq(color = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.15, size = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ n_label, nrow = 2) +
  labs(title = "Normal Q-Q Plots", x = "Theoretical Quantiles", y = "Sample Quantiles") +
  tight_theme

# Combine side-by-side with tight layout
p_dens_tight | p_qq_tight
```

- **Density Overlays:** As seen in the density charts, there is no noticeable change not explained by randomness as the sample size grows.
  <!-- Mention the alignment with the standard N(0, 1) curve. Include or reference density_vs_normal_2x3_grid.png -->
- **Q-Q Plot Quantile Alignment:** Similarly to the graphs for density, there is no noticeable change not explained by randomness for the Q-Q plots. They demonstrate very linearly from n = 1.
  <!-- Inspect the linearity in your exported Q-Q plots from qq_plots_by_n/. -->

### Statistical Evidence (Shapiro-Wilk Test & Moment Ratios)

```{r}
#| label: tbl-normality-metrics
#| tbl-cap: "Normality assessment metrics: Skewness, Kurtosis, and Shapiro-Wilk test."

summary_table %>%
  select(n, skewness, excess_kurtosis, shapiro_stat_W, shapiro_p_value) %>%
  kable(col.names = c("n", "Skewness", "Excess Kurtosis", "Shapiro-Wilk W", "p-value")) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"))
```

- **Conclusion on Normality:**
  <!-- Summarize when the distribution meets practical and formal normality thresholds. -->
  Looking at this data we can see that from n=1, the data is very
  normalized. The Shapiro-Wilk W of 0.9998 (approaches 1 at perfect
  normality) is very high indicating a highly measurable normal. As
  mentioned previously in this analysis, the skewness and excess
  kurtosis readings are very close to 0 indicating a normalized curve.
  The high p-value is evidence that we cannot reject the null hypothesis
  of our distribution being normalized.

## 7. Limitations and Surprises

<!-- Question 7: What limitations or surprises did you observe? -->

- **Key Observations / Surprises:** There were not really any surprises with this one. I was expecting the Monte Carlo randomness to provide more variability but possibly in other set seeds there is more.
  <!-- e.g., persistent tail skewness, boundary effects, Shapiro-Wilk p-value sensitivity to large sample sizes, etc. -->
- **Simulation Limitations:** I don't think there were many limitations associated with this distribution as the data appeared to converge right away. If there was a limit to Monte Carlo reps maybe a lower number would not have such a smoothing effect and it would show visually and statistically. 
  <!-- e.g., finite Monte Carlo reps B = 10,000, fixed selection of n_values, truncation of sub-sample size for normality testing. -->

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 8. Final Verdict

#### Central Limit Theorem Confirmed at *n = 1*

Unsurprisingly the Standard Normal distribution conforms to central
limit theorem from n=1. Based on both visual analysis and statistical
analysis I feel comfortable confirming this fact.
